jd:
HVAC / refrigeration engineer
Junior to mid
Commercial and light-industrial refrigeration contractor. Engineers size and check vapor-compression systems for cold rooms and process chillers, document cycle performance using EU nomenclature (cooling EER and heat-pump COP, both in W/W), and compare real machines to an ideal Carnot benchmark for design reviews and client reports.

Day to day:
- Build thermodynamic state-point tables for vapor-compression cycles from design temperatures and refrigerant data
- Look up refrigerant properties from tables, software, or online tools and document the source
- Calculate refrigerating effect, compressor work, cooling EER, and heat-pump COP including compression efficiency
- Compare cycle performance to an inverse Carnot reference that accounts for heat-exchanger temperature differences
- Write clear calculation notes a senior engineer can review without guessing assumptions

Required skills:
- Can define evaporator, compressor, condenser, and expansion states for a simple vapor-compression cycle
- Comfortable reading R22 (or similar) thermodynamic properties from tables or property software
- Can apply isentropic and actual compression work with a given compression efficiency
- Understands EU EER (cooling, W/W), COP (heating, W/W), and the inverse Carnot refrigerator benchmark

Nice to have:
- Familiarity with CoolProp, REFPROP, or manufacturer property software
- Experience with p-h diagrams and suction-line superheat conventions
- Prior cold-room or commercial refrigeration design work

Constraints:
- Assessment is a thermodynamics calculation work sample — not building production software
- Candidates may use any tools they like for refrigerant properties and arithmetic
- Do not require paid licensed software beyond what is freely available on the desktop or online
- Starter files on the desktop are shared scenery (parameters and a blank calculation template), not a solved answer
prompt: You are checking the thermodynamic performance of a simple vapor-compression system using R22. The same machine may cool (refrigeration) or heat (heat pump). Design data are fixed below. Using EU nomenclature (EN 14511-style steady-state metrics), produce a clear calculation of cooling EER and heat-pump COP — both in W/W — then compare cooling performance to an inverse Carnot cycle with a 9 K temperature difference at both the evaporator and the condenser. You are free to use any tools you like (spreadsheets, calculators, CoolProp/REFPROP, ASHRAE or manufacturer tables, online property tools, etc.) to obtain R22 properties — document which source you used.
